t: The tendency of persons who face higher-than-average risk to seek insurance more actively than low-risk persons is called:
e: Adverse selection (anti-selection) is the pull of poor risks towards insurance; underwriting exists largely to counter it. Morale hazard is carelessness caused by the existence of insurance.

t: Under which Section of the Insurance Act, 1938 is an insurer prohibited from assuming risk unless the premium is received in advance?
e: Section 64VB requires premium to be received in advance before risk commencement, subject to prescribed exceptions. Section 64UM deals with surveyors and Section 45 with life policies.

t: Which characteristic makes a risk commercially insurable?
o: Losses should be catastrophic so that premium is high
Loss should be definite, measurable and accidental
Exposure units should be few and dissimilar
The insured should be able to control when the loss occurs
e: An insurable risk needs a large number of homogeneous exposures, losses that are fortuitous, definite and measurable, and premium that is economically feasible; catastrophic or controllable losses defeat pooling.

t: The Tariff Advisory Committee, which earlier controlled rates and wordings for tariff classes in India, was abolished by:
e: After de-tariffing from 1 January 2007, the TAC's functions became redundant and the Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015 abolished it, transferring residual functions to IRDAI.

t: A fire underwriter receives a proposal for a chemical plant with sum insured of ₹120 crore. The most appropriate next step before quoting is to:
o: Refer the proposal to the Insurance Ombudsman
Decline the risk since chemical plants are uninsurable
Issue the policy at the manual rate and verify later
Arrange a pre-acceptance risk inspection and obtain a survey report
e: Large or hazardous risks are inspected before acceptance so the underwriter can assess construction, process hazards, protection and PML. Declining or blind acceptance are both poor practice.

t: Which document is issued as evidence of cover when the policy cannot be issued immediately, usually for a limited period?
e: A cover note is a temporary document confirming that cover has commenced pending issue of the policy; in motor insurance it is valid for a limited period.

t: A proposer for a burglary policy on a jewellery shop fails to mention two burglary claims in the previous three years. If a loss occurs, the insurer can:
o: Avoid the policy for non-disclosure of a material fact
Do nothing because claims history is not a material fact
Recover the loss from the police
e: Previous loss experience is a material fact; non-disclosure breaches utmost good faith and makes the contract voidable at the insurer's option.

t: The main difference between an 'excess' and a 'franchise' is that:
o: Under a franchise the insurer pays the full loss once the loss exceeds the stated amount, whereas under an excess the stated amount is always deducted
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
A franchise is always expressed as a percentage and an excess always as a rupee amount
An excess applies only to motor policies and a franchise only to marine
e: With a franchise, losses below the threshold are not paid but losses above it are paid in full; with an excess (deductible) the amount is deducted from every claim.

t: A health insurer loads premium by 20% for a proposer with controlled hypertension instead of declining. This is an example of:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Individual risk features that deviate from the standard class are handled through loadings, exclusions or restrictions rather than outright declinature.

t: Which of the following is NOT one of the regulatory objectives of insurance rates?
o: Rates should be identical for all insurers
Rates should not be unfairly discriminatory
e: The classical rate-making objectives are adequacy, non-excessiveness and fairness; in a de-tariffed market rates differ between insurers based on their own experience and costs.

t: The 'pure premium' in rate making represents:
o: Expected losses per unit of exposure, before any loading for expenses or profit
e: Pure premium (loss cost) = expected frequency × expected severity per exposure unit; expenses, profit and contingency loadings are added to obtain the gross rate.

t: An insurer's data for a class of risk shows 4,000 vehicle-years of exposure, 320 claims and total incurred losses of ₹9.6 crore. The pure premium per vehicle-year is:
e: Pure premium = total losses ÷ exposure = ₹9,60,00,000 ÷ 4,000 = ₹24,000. Equivalently frequency (0.08) × severity (₹3,00,000) = ₹24,000.

t: The statistical principle that allows insurers to predict aggregate losses with greater accuracy as the number of similar exposures increases is:
e: The law of large numbers states that actual results approach expected results as the number of independent, homogeneous exposures grows; it underpins pooling and rate making.

t: 'Earned premium' for a financial year is best defined as:
o: Total premium collected during the year
Premium written during the year minus commission
Premium attributable to the portion of the policy periods that fell within the year
e: Earned premium = written premium adjusted for the change in unexpired risk reserve, i.e. only the part of premium for cover actually provided in the year counts as earned.

t: A one-year fire policy with premium of ₹24,000 is issued on 1 October 2025. On 31 March 2026, the earned premium and unearned premium (1/365 basis, ignoring the extra day) are approximately:
e: Six months of the twelve-month term have elapsed, so half the premium (₹12,000) is earned and half remains unearned.

t: Class rating (manual rating) is most suitable when:
o: The insurer has no loss data at all
There is a large number of homogeneous risks with similar loss characteristics
Each risk is unique with no comparable exposures
e: Class rating applies an average rate to all risks in a homogeneous class, which works well for mass lines such as motor and health where large numbers allow credible averages.

t: Under schedule rating, the final rate for a fire risk is derived by:
o: Starting from a base rate and applying charges and credits for specific physical features of the risk
Using only the insured's own past losses
Applying the market average rate uniformly
e: Schedule rating modifies a base rate with debits for adverse features (hazardous occupancy, poor construction) and credits for good features (sprinklers, hydrants).

t: Experience rating differs from retrospective rating in that:
o: Retrospective rating ignores actual losses entirely
Experience rating never uses credibility factors
Retrospective rating is used only in fire insurance
Experience rating uses the insured's past losses to adjust the current premium, whereas retrospective rating adjusts the premium of the policy period itself based on losses during that period
e: Experience rating is prospective (past losses modify future premium); retrospective rating is settled after the policy expires using the actual losses of that same period, within a minimum and maximum.

t: Under IRDAI's 2024 health insurance norms, the maximum waiting period that an insurer may impose for pre-existing diseases is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). The maximum PED waiting period was reduced from 48 to 36 months, and the moratorium period after which claims cannot be contested (except fraud) was reduced to 60 months.

t: A fleet is placed on a retrospective rating plan with basic premium ₹6 lakh, loss conversion factor 1.10, tax multiplier 1.05, minimum premium ₹8 lakh and maximum premium ₹20 lakh. Incurred losses for the year are ₹10 lakh. The retrospective premium payable is:
e: Retro premium = (B + L×c) × T = (6 + 10×1.10) × 1.05 = 17 × 1.05 = ₹17.85 lakh, which lies between the minimum and maximum, so it is payable as calculated.

t: In the pure premium method of rate making, if pure premium is ₹3,000 per unit, fixed expense per unit is ₹300, variable expenses are 25% of gross premium and the profit and contingency loading is 5%, the indicated gross rate is:
e: Gross rate = (pure premium + fixed expense) ÷ (1 − variable expense ratio − profit loading) = 3,300 ÷ (1 − 0.25 − 0.05) = 3,300 ÷ 0.70 = ₹4,714 (rounded).

t: Which exposure base is normally used for pricing a workmen's/employees' compensation policy?
o: Annual wages of the employees covered
e: Employees' compensation liability is linked to wages, so premium is charged as a rate on the estimated annual wages, adjusted at expiry if actual wages differ.

t: The 'File and Use' system introduced by IRDA for general insurance products required insurers to:
o: Obtain approval from the General Insurance Council
Use only tariff wordings with no filing
Launch a product first and inform the Authority afterwards
File the product with the Authority and use it only after the specified waiting period or clearance
e: Under File and Use, the product, rates and wordings had to be filed with IRDA before use, and the insurer could market it only after the Authority's clearance or expiry of the prescribed period without objection.

t: De-tariffing of general insurance rates in India became effective from:
e: IRDA freed pricing for the erstwhile tariff classes (fire, engineering, motor OD, workmen's compensation, etc.) from 1 January 2007, while Motor third-party rates remained regulated.

t: Under the erstwhile fire tariff short-period scale, a policy issued for three months attracted 40% of the annual premium. An insured takes a fire policy on stock for three months with annual rate giving ₹60,000 per annum. The premium charged is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Short-period premium = 40% of ₹60,000 = ₹24,000, which exceeds the pro-rata amount of ₹15,000 for a quarter.

t: Even after de-tariffing, which premium continues to be notified by the regulator/government rather than freely priced by insurers?
e: Motor TP liability premium is prescribed annually (now notified by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways in consultation with IRDAI) because the cover is compulsory under the Motor Vehicles Act.

t: Under the File and Use regime, the person responsible for certifying that the rates filed are adequate and based on sound actuarial principles is the insurer's:
e: The Appointed Actuary certifies the technical basis, adequacy and fairness of premium rates filed; the CEO certifies compliance with regulations.

topic: Applications of File and Use and Use and File Procedures
t: The key distinction of the 'Use and File' procedure as compared with 'File and Use' is that:
o: Products need no filing at all
Only IRDAI can design the product
The insurer may launch the product after internal approval and file it with IRDAI within the prescribed period after launch
Products must be re-filed every month
e: Use and File allows an insurer to launch a product following approval by its Product Management Committee and then file it with the Authority, speeding up product introduction.

topic: Applications of File and Use and Use and File Procedures
t: A general insurer wishes to launch a new add-on cover for electric vehicle batteries under the Use and File procedure. Which internal body must approve the product before launch?
e: Use and File requires sign-off by the insurer's Product Management Committee (including the Appointed Actuary and risk/compliance heads) before the product is used and then filed.

topic: Applications of File and Use and Use and File Procedures
t: Which of the following statements about product filing in India is INCORRECT?
o: Rates for Motor TP liability are set through the product filing of each insurer
Products filed must comply with the IRDAI (Insurance Products) Regulations, 2024
A board-approved underwriting policy is a prerequisite for the insurer
Use and File was extended to most general and health insurance products in 2022
e: Motor TP premium is not freely filed by insurers; it is notified by the government in consultation with IRDAI. The other statements correctly describe the current framework.

t: A pre-acceptance risk inspection report is most valuable to the underwriter because it:
o: Provides first-hand verification of construction, occupancy, protection and exposure that the proposal form may not fully disclose
Replaces the need for a proposal form
e: Risk inspection independently confirms and supplements the proposer's disclosures, enabling correct classification, loading or credit and recommendations for risk improvement.

t: A warranty in a general insurance policy is:
o: A condition that must be strictly complied with by the insured, breach of which allows the insurer to avoid liability
An optional recommendation by the surveyor
A promise by the insurer to pay all claims
A clause that increases the sum insured automatically
e: Warranties (e.g. maintenance of fire extinguishers, no storage of hazardous goods) are underwriting tools that control hazard; breach entitles the insurer to repudiate, irrespective of connection with the loss unless the policy says otherwise.

t: Which of the following is NOT a method of risk control that an underwriter may insist upon?
o: Retention of all losses by the insurer at no premium
Segregation of hazardous processes by fire walls
Round-the-clock security at a cash counter
e: Risk control measures include loss prevention and reduction devices and procedures. An insurer absorbing losses without premium is neither a control nor an underwriting tool.

t: A fire insurer uses a surplus treaty of 10 lines with net retention of ₹1 crore per risk. A risk of ₹8 crore is accepted. What is the maximum amount ceded to the treaty, and what further arrangement is needed, if any?
o: ₹7 crore ceded; no further arrangement needed
₹7 crore ceded; facultative cover needed for the balance
e: Treaty capacity is 10 lines × ₹1 crore = ₹10 crore beyond retention. After retaining ₹1 crore, ₹7 crore goes to the treaty, within capacity, so no facultative placement is needed.

t: The IRDAI portal through which a policyholder can escalate an unresolved grievance against an insurer is:
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Bima Bharosa (formerly IGMS) is the grievance portal; Bima Sugam is the marketplace, Bima Vahak the women-led distribution channel and Bima Vistaar the combined rural product.

t: 'Probable Maximum Loss' (PML) is used by underwriters mainly to:
o: Decide retention and reinsurance requirements for a large risk
Calculate the premium payable by the insured
Determine the claim payable after a loss
e: PML is an estimate of the largest loss likely from a single event on a risk; it guides how much the insurer retains and how much it needs to reinsure.

t: Under the Standard Fire and Special Perils policy wording, which of the following perils required an add-on cover rather than being included as a basic peril?
o: Bursting and overflowing of water tanks
e: Earthquake (fire and shock) is an add-on to the standard fire policy; lightning, impact damage and bursting of water tanks are among the named basic perils.

t: A 'declaration policy' in fire insurance is designed for:
o: Stocks whose value fluctuates frequently during the policy period
e: Declaration policies cover fluctuating stocks: a provisional premium is charged on the maximum sum insured and adjusted at expiry based on periodic declarations of actual stock values.

t: A reinstatement value policy differs from a standard (market value) fire policy because:
o: It pays only the depreciated value of the property
It pays the cost of replacing the damaged property with new property of the same kind, without deduction for depreciation
e: Reinstatement value cover is used for buildings, plant and machinery and pays replacement cost as new, subject to reinstatement actually being carried out; stocks are not covered on this basis.

t: Institute Cargo Clauses (A) differ from Clauses (B) and (C) in that Clauses (A):
o: Provide the widest cover on an 'all risks' basis subject to exclusions
Are used only for inland transit
e: ICC (A) is an all-risks form subject to stated exclusions; ICC (B) and (C) are named-peril covers with (C) being the narrowest.

t: In a private car package policy, the Insured's Declared Value (IDV) of a vehicle aged between 2 and 3 years is arrived at by applying a depreciation of:
e: The IDV depreciation schedule is 5% (up to 6 months), 15% (6 months–1 year), 20% (1–2 years), 30% (2–3 years), 40% (3–4 years) and 50% (4–5 years) on the manufacturer's listed selling price.

t: An insurer's portfolio shows net earned premium ₹500 crore, net incurred claims ₹380 crore and management expenses plus net commission of ₹140 crore. The combined ratio is:
e: Combined ratio = (incurred claims + expenses) ÷ net earned premium = (380 + 140) ÷ 500 = 104%, indicating an underwriting loss of 4% before investment income.

t: An insurer must resolve a policyholder's grievance within how many days of receipt?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). 14 days under the 2024 regulations; thereafter the policyholder may approach Bima Bharosa or the Ombudsman.

t: A combined ratio of less than 100% indicates that the insurer:
o: Has made an underwriting profit before investment income
Has not met the solvency margin
e: When claims plus expenses are less than earned premium, the underwriting account is in profit; above 100% the insurer depends on investment income to remain profitable.

t: Which action is a typical re-underwriting strategy for a portfolio of commercial fire risks with deteriorating loss ratios?
o: Reducing deductibles across the board to attract more business
Stopping all risk inspections to save cost
Reviewing each renewal for loss history, imposing risk-improvement warranties and re-pricing or exiting consistently loss-making accounts
e: Re-underwriting means systematically reviewing an existing book at renewal to correct pricing, terms and selection; the other options would worsen results.

t: The 'underwriting cycle' refers to:
o: The alternation between soft markets (low rates, ample capacity) and hard markets (rising rates, restricted capacity)
The annual renewal calendar of policies
The sequence of proposal, inspection and policy issue
e: The underwriting cycle describes market-wide swings in pricing and capacity driven by competition, capital and loss experience; underwriters must price with discipline through the cycle.

t: As per IRDAI's Master Circular on Protection of Policyholders' Interests (2024), the free-look period available to a policyholder for policies with a term of one year or more is:
e: The 2024 framework provides a uniform free-look period of 30 days from receipt of the policy document, extended from the earlier 15 days.

t: Under the Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017 as amended, the maximum value of a complaint (including relief claimed) that the Insurance Ombudsman can entertain is:
e: The 2021 amendment to the Ombudsman Rules raised the monetary ceiling of complaints to ₹50 lakh, and the award is binding on the insurer.

topic: Research and Development in Underwriting, Rating and Product Innovation
t: Parametric (index-based) insurance differs from traditional indemnity insurance because:
o: Payment is triggered when a pre-defined index (e.g. rainfall below a threshold) is breached, without loss assessment
Claims are paid on proof of actual loss after survey
It is available only for motor risks
e: Parametric covers pay a pre-agreed amount on an objective trigger, giving speed and lower claims cost but introducing basis risk; weather-index crop covers in India are an example.

t: The Insurance Information Bureau of India (IIB) assists underwriters primarily by:
o: Fixing premium rates for all insurers
Maintaining industry-wide databases (e.g. motor and health) that help verify claims history and detect fraud
Settling claims on behalf of insurers
e: IIB, promoted by IRDAI, collects and shares industry data such as motor vehicle and claim records, enabling underwriters to check history, NCB and fraud patterns.
